Futures basics before using a signal

Long, short, margin, leverage, stops, and targets explained without a profit promise.

Contract Compass guide · Updated November 6, 2026

A futures contract gives exposure to an asset’s price without being the same thing as buying that asset in a spot wallet. Contract Compass reads public Binance USDT perpetual-market data. It neither opens an exchange account nor checks whether a particular product is available or suitable where you live.

Long and short describe exposure

A long position generally gains from a rise in price and loses from a fall, before trading costs. A short position has the opposite price exposure. Fees, funding, and execution prices also affect the result. A short is not a way to avoid risk when the market looks uncertain.

On this site, “Buy / Long” and “Sell / Short” label conditional scenarios. Only the separate live decision indicates whether the app’s rules currently agree. Read How to read the decision signal before treating a scenario as actionable evidence.

Margin and leverage are different from a loss limit

Margin is money committed to support a position. Leverage describes a position that is larger than the margin set aside. That magnifies exposure relative to the money committed: a relatively small adverse price move can have a large effect on the account.

The exchange can close a position when its margin requirements are no longer satisfied. This is liquidation. The margin shown by this app is not a liquidation estimate, and a calculator’s loss budget is not a guarantee that the account cannot lose more.

Entry, stop, and target are a plan

An entry is the price at which exposure starts. A stop is intended to close exposure when the trade moves against the plan. A target is a planned favorable exit. Stops can fill at worse prices during fast moves, while targets may never be reached.

A completed-candle breakout and the eventual execution price are different observations. Even if the candle confirms a level, the market may have moved beyond a sensible entry by the time you look. Contract Compass can remove a signal when its live price is extended, loses the breakout, crosses the stop, or reaches its first target.

Understand the costs separately

The calculator includes editable assumptions for fees and slippage. The market overview also displays a funding rate and can flag funding within the chosen holding window. Funding is variable and is excluded from the sizing calculation. Do not read a positive or negative funding rate as a standalone entry signal.

Practice reading before risking money

Use fictional balances to compare price distance, quantity, margin, and loss at the stop. Explain in your own words which conditions have passed and which remain unconfirmed. If you cannot explain why the decision is available, pause instead of increasing leverage.

This site is educational technical analysis, not personalized investment advice. It does not consider your income, debts, total positions, or ability to absorb a loss. CFTC: risks of virtual-currency trading. The advisory explains why virtual-currency derivatives and leverage deserve particular care.
